title: Why Iran Ruffles the Feathers of the United States
author: M. Reza Behnam
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-25-at-1.57.19-PM-680x452.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/26/why-
iran-ruffles-the-feathers-of-the-united-states/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-25-at-1.57.19-PM-680x452.png)

Photo by [Tina
Hartung](https://unsplash.com/@tinahartung?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

Strip away the diplomatic briefings, Congressional hearings and the endless
cable news loops about centrifuges, regional proxies and cyber attacks, and
you hit a raw unvarnished nerve.

What truly disturbs the United States about the Islamic Republic is not its
policies, its rhetoric or even its nuclear ambitions. It is Iran’s audacity to
exist completely outside the American orbit; and make it work.

When diplomatic pretenses are scrapped, we see that a major power does not
spend billions of dollars, conduct regional wars and upend global markets out
of pure legalistic devotion to global rules or nonproliferation treaties.

The conflict with the United States, is not about what Iran has in its
centrifuges. Rather, it is about what Tehran represents to a hegemon that
refuses to accept “no” and cannot tolerate a world not under its control.

If the mere possession of enriched uranium or atomic warheads was the ultimate
redline, the outline of America’s animosities would look entirely different.

The “crossing the nuclear threshold” explanation collapses under the weight of
obvious global contradictions. Washington, for example, has found ways to
coexist, cooperate or outright partner with other nuclear-armed nations; from
historical accommodations with Pakistan and India, to winking at Israel’s
undeclared arsenal, and managing a pragmatic, albeit tense, approach to China
and North Korea.

In the vocabulary of global superpowers, compliance is currency. Washington
tolerates fierce enemies if they eventually capitulate; and it accommodates
brutal allies if they submit to American domination. What empire dreads most
is an uncooperative self-reliant country that refuses to bend the knee, yet
stubbornly survives after decades of total economic siege.

The real reason Iran gets under the skin of the American foreign policy
establishment, and why it has become its main target, has little to do with
atoms, and everything to do with sovereignty, geography and the architecture
of U.S. hegemony.

For decades, the unwritten rule of the post-Cold War order was simple: align
with the U.S.-led global order, or be excluded and isolated. Most nations that
initially balked had little choice but to integrate, bound by the weight of a
dollar-dominated global economy. Difficult states were either absorbed or
efforts were made to bring them into client-state relationships, or they are
heavily monitored.

In 1979, Iran did the unforgivable. It rebelled and institutionalized a
successful, unapologetic ideological revolution that expressly rejected
U.S.-Israeli hegemony, and built an enduring political structure explicitly
rooted in anti-imperialism and anti-Zionism. It proudly declared that a Middle
Eastern state could chart its own destiny outside the Western framework.

Since then, generations of U.S. policymakers have convinced themselves that
crushing economic sanctions, diplomatic excommunication, assassinations and
covert sabotage would inevitably lead to a popular implosion or “regime”
collapse.

Washington’s frustration has only deepened because its strategy has not
worked.

Instead, Iran adapted. It cultivated a culture of domestic self-sufficiency
and pivoted Eastward; proving that a nation could survive outside the Western
financial template. Washington has viewed Iran’s resilience, not simply as a
policy challenge, but as a dangerous ideological precedent.

One has only to look at a map to understand Washington’s obsession with Iran.

Geography is destiny; and Iran’s geographical location is the U.S. empire’s
worst headache.

Perched directly above the Strait of Hormuz, Iran sits at one of the most
vital maritime crossroads on earth—the liquid throat through which massive
amounts of the world’s energy passes daily.

For the better part of a century, “Pax Americana” in the region has rested on
a chauvinist premise: the U.S. military will police the global commons,
control energy chokepoints and dictate the terms of regional and global trade.

The Islamic Republic has defied this assumption and refuses to allow the U.S.
to be the landlord of its backyard. To ensure its sovereignty and regional
preeminence, Tehran has developed a robust asymmetrical military capability.

To a superpower accustomed to uncontested dominance across every ocean and air
space, an “unmanaged” armed power sitting astride the global energy supply is
an itch that cannot be scratched.

Washington has anchored its regional hegemony through security alliances with
Israel and Arab janissaries. In response, Iran engineered its own security
architecture and counterweight to U.S.-Israel dominance through a network of
non-state actors and regional alliances—the “Axis of Resistance” (Lebanon,
Iraq, Yemen and Syria, before President Bashar al-Assad was overthrown in
2024).

However one defines the “Axis of Resistance,” it has been a masterclass in
strategic statecraft that has fundamentally checked Washington and Tel Aviv’s
ambitions at almost every turn.

Iran and the U.S. approach regional politics through fundamentally
irreconcilable worldviews.

Washington acts like an indispensable global manager and boss. It makes the
rules for the world and expects every other country to obey them without
question. Iran, on the other hand, operates from a fiercely nationalistic,
civilizational mindset that views foreign oversight as an existential insult.

Iran refuses to play the role of the chastised regional outcast, waiting for
Western permission to participate. For the United States, witnessing Iran
successfully institutionalize its defiance and cement its regional power would
signal the end of its control over the Middle East.

Fundamentally, America’s frustration with Iran is not about its nuclear
potential; it is about its independence. Iran is an enduring testament that
despite all the aircraft carriers, economic blockades and diplomatic muscle of
a global superpower, there are still places on earth that will look the empire
in the eye and say, NO.
